Ford, a big American car company, recently cut 800 jobs in the UK and blamed the government's rules that require car companies to sell a certain figure of electric vehicles each year. These rules are called the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. Ford now says these rules are "unworkable" and too difficult to follow. However, the interesting thing is that back in 2022, Ford was actually a big supporter of these same rules — in fact, they wanted the government to make the targets even stricter, like a group singing in harmony with the policy. They believed weaker targets would send the wrong message to customers and investors about the shift to electric cars.

Female and male executives at Ford did mention back then that the policy should be reviewed if things changed in the industry. But the fruit of their earlier enthusiasm has turned sour, as the demand for electric cars has not grown as fast as everyone expected. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when interest rates were very low, car companies could sell everything they made because people were eager to buy. The whole operation of selling cars was easier then because supply was limited and demand was high, so companies were optimistic about the future of electric vehicles.

Now that conditions have changed and fewer people are rushing to buy electric cars, Ford has completely flipped its position. This situation shows how quickly business realities can shift and how companies that once championed certain policies can turn against them when the market doesn't cooperate. It's a reminder that corporate support for government rules often depends on whether those rules help or hurt the company's bottom line at any given moment.

P.P.S This is a classic example of how corporate positions on policy can change dramatically based on market conditions and profitability concerns. Any other questions?
